claim: Animals mimicking other organisms or using camouflage to deceive predators are vital survival strategies.
source: Animals mimicking other organisms or using camouflage to deceive predators are vital survival strategies.
evidence: This is a general statement about animal behavior that draws from established scientific understanding of mimicry and camouflage as survival strategies.

claim: Modern and fossil insects can simulate diverse objects.
source: Modern and fossil insects can simulate diverse objects.
evidence: This statement reflects established knowledge about insect mimicry documented in both modern and fossil records.

claim: Lichens are an ancient symbiosis between a fungus and an alga or a cyanobacterium.
source: Lichens are an ancient symbiosis between a fungus and an alga or a cyanobacterium that sometimes have a plant-like appearance and occasionally are mimicked by modern animals.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about the nature of lichens as symbiotic organisms.

claim: Lichen models are almost absent in the fossil record of mimicry.
source: Nevertheless, lichen models are almost absent in fossil record of mimicry.
evidence: This statement is based on inference from the existing fossil record and literature on mimicry.

claim: This study provides the earliest fossil evidence of a mimetic relationship between the moth lacewing mimic Lichenipolystoechotes gen. nov. and its co-occurring fossil lichen model Daohugouthallus ciliiferus.
source: Here, we provide the earliest fossil evidence of a mimetic relationship between the moth lacewing mimic Lichenipolystoechotes gen. nov. and its co-occurring fossil lichen model Daohugouthallus ciliiferus.
evidence: This claim is supported by the fossil specimens described in the manuscript, including morphological comparisons and measurements.

claim: The lichen affinity of D. ciliiferus is corroborated by structural similarities and detailed measurements.
source: We corroborate the lichen affinity of D. ciliiferus and document this mimetic relationship by providing structural similarities and detailed measurements of the mimic's wing and correspondingly the model's thallus.
evidence: This is supported by SEM observations and morphological measurements presented in the manuscript.

claim: The discovery of lichen mimesis predates modern lichen-insect associations by 165 million years.
source: Our discovery of lichen mimesis predates modern lichen-insect associations by 165 million years, indicating that during the mid-Mesozoic, the lichen-insect mimesis system was well established and provided lacewings with highly honed survival strategies.
evidence: This is based on the age of the fossil deposit (168-152 Ma) and comparison with modern associations.

claim: During the mid-Mesozoic, the lichen-insect mimesis system was well established.
source: Our discovery of lichen mimesis predates modern lichen-insect associations by 165 million years, indicating that during the mid-Mesozoic, the lichen-insect mimesis system was well established and provided lacewings with highly honed survival strategies.
evidence: This is inferred from the fossil evidence of mimicry presented in the study.

claim: Katydids and butterflies mimic leaves.
source: For instance, the specializations occurring in katydids and butterflies that mimic leaves, stick insects and inchworms that resemble twigs, and orchid mantids that duplicate orchid flowers, provide ecological insights for understanding mimetic associations between insect mimics and their plant models (Stevens, 2011; Gullan and Cranston, 2014; Maran, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature on insect mimicry.

claim: Stick insects and inchworms resemble twigs.
source: For instance, the specializations occurring in katydids and butterflies that mimic leaves, stick insects and inchworms that resemble twigs, and orchid mantids that duplicate orchid flowers, provide ecological insights for understanding mimetic associations between insect mimics and their plant models (Stevens, 2011; Gullan and Cranston, 2014; Maran, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature on insect mimicry.

claim: Orchid mantids duplicate orchid flowers.
source: For instance, the specializations occurring in katydids and butterflies that mimic leaves, stick insects and inchworms that resemble twigs, and orchid mantids that duplicate orchid flowers, provide ecological insights for understanding mimetic associations between insect mimics and their plant models (Stevens, 2011; Gullan and Cranston, 2014; Maran, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature on insect mimicry.

claim: Mimesis or camouflage is highly effective when cryptic insects resemble closely the appropriate self-similar background.
source: These and other fascinating cases reveal that mimesis or camouflage is highly effective when cryptic insects resemble closely the appropriate self-similar background, indicating the complexity of ecological relationships between insect mimics and their imitating models.
evidence: This is inferred from the examples of mimicry cited and represents established understanding in the field.

claim: A Permian katydid exhibiting a mimicking pattern of wings similar to modern relatives was considered the oldest case of insect mimicry.
source: A Permian katydid exhibiting a mimicking pattern of wings similar to the modern relatives was considered the oldest case of insect mimicry (Garrouste et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Garrouste et al., 2016.

claim: Evidence for a contemporaneous mimetic relationship in the Permian deposit was scarce.
source: However, evidence for a contemporaneous mimetic relationship in this Permian deposit was scarce, and there was no quantitative or other useful data to track the mimetic interactions among the insect, model and predator.
evidence: This is an inference based on evaluation of the cited Permian study.

claim: Several Mesozoic insect taxa developed remarkable structural adaptations resulting in highly accurate resemblances to co-existing models.
source: As in morphological specializations involving masterly deceit found in modern insects, several Mesozoic insect taxa developed remarkable structural adaptations resulting in highly accurate resemblances to co-existing models (Wang et al., 2012; Wang et al., 2014; Yang et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies on Mesozoic insect mimicry.

claim: Neuroptera consists of ca. 6000 extant species.
source: Prominent among these mimetic insects are Neuroptera (lacewings, antlions and relatives), a nonspeciose relic order consisting of ca. 6000 extant species that engaged in several, impressive instances of mimicry that reveal novel and specialized strategies of deception, of which many are absent today.
evidence: This is established taxonomic knowledge about the diversity of Neuroptera.

claim: The Jurassic lacewing Bellinympha (Saucrosmylidae) mimicked cycadophyte leaves.
source: Striking examples are the Jurassic lacewing Bellinympha (Saucrosmylidae), a compression fossil, mimicking cycadophyte leaves (Wang et al., 2010b), and larvae of the green lacewing Phyllochrysa (Chrysopidae) from amber, modified to resemble co-occurring liverworts (Liu et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Wang et al., 2010b.

claim: Larvae of the green lacewing Phyllochrysa (Chrysopidae) from amber were modified to resemble co-occurring liverworts.
source: Striking examples are the Jurassic lacewing Bellinympha (Saucrosmylidae), a compression fossil, mimicking cycadophyte leaves (Wang et al., 2010b), and larvae of the green lacewing Phyllochrysa (Chrysopidae) from amber, modified to resemble co-occurring liverworts (Liu et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Liu et al., 2018.

claim: Camouflaged larvae of chrysopid and myrmeleontoid neuropterans in amber evolved distinctive debris-carrying behaviors to enhance their predatory effectiveness.
source: Besides mimicry, other deceptive modes of appearance have been documented among Mesozoic lacewings, such as camouflaged larvae of chrysopid (green lacewing) and myrmeleontoid (antlion relative) neuropterans in amber, which evolved distinctive debris-carrying behaviors to enhance their predatory effectiveness (Pérez-de la Fuente et al., 2012; Pérez-de la Fuente et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2016; Badano et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to published studies on Mesozoic lacewing larvae.

claim: The new lichen-like-mimicking insects are from the Daohugou 1 locality of Inner Mongolia in northeastern China.
source: These occurrences are from the Daohugou 1 locality of Inner Mongolia in northeastern China.
evidence: This is based on the collection locality of the specimens described in the study.

claim: The new lichen-like-mimicking insects represent a new genus with two new species.
source: The new lichen-like-mimicking insects represent a new genus with two new species and exhibit remarkable wing patterns that accurately resemble the contemporaneous lichen species Daohugouthallus ciliiferus Wang, Krings et Taylor, 2010 (Wang et al., 2010a).
evidence: This is based on the taxonomic description and analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: The new insects exhibit remarkable wing patterns that accurately resemble the contemporaneous lichen species Daohugouthallus ciliiferus.
source: The new lichen-like-mimicking insects represent a new genus with two new species and exhibit remarkable wing patterns that accurately resemble the contemporaneous lichen species Daohugouthallus ciliiferus Wang, Krings et Taylor, 2010 (Wang et al., 2010a).
evidence: This is supported by morphological comparisons and measurements presented in the manuscript.

claim: The lichen affinity of D. ciliiferus was previously doubted due to the absence of evidence for fungal and algal connections.
source: The lichen affinity of the D. ciliiferus model previously was doubted due to the absence of evidence for fungal and algal connections that would indicate the presence of lichenization and thus the presence of a mutualistic symbiosis (Honegger et al., 2013; Lücking and Nelsen, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Honegger et al., 2013 and Lücking and Nelsen, 2018.

claim: SEM results corroborate the actual presence of hyphae connected to algal cells on the D. ciliiferus specimens.
source: Our SEM results corroborate the actual presence of hyphae connected to algal cells on the D. ciliiferus specimens, indicating the foliose and subfruticose lichen growth forms were in existence during the Middle Jurassic.
evidence: This is supported by SEM observations presented in Figure 2 of the manuscript.

claim: Foliose and subfruticose lichen growth forms were in existence during the Middle Jurassic.
source: Our SEM results corroborate the actual presence of hyphae connected to algal cells on the D. ciliiferus specimens, indicating the foliose and subfruticose lichen growth forms were in existence during the Middle Jurassic.
evidence: This is inferred from the SEM observations of D. ciliiferus specimens.

claim: Present-day lichen-mimicking insects are widely recorded among Coleoptera, Lepidoptera, and Orthoptera.
source: Present-day lichen-mimicking insects are widely recorded among several diverse orders, especially Coleoptera (beetles), Lepidoptera (moths and butterflies) and Orthoptera (grasshoppers, katydids and crickets), which have evolved unusual specializations of morphology and behavior consistent with co-occurring lichens and other habitation- or appearance similar organisms such as liverworts (Gerson, 1973; Lücking, 2001; Capinera, 2008; Cannon, 2010; Lücking et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to published literature on lichen-mimicking insects.

claim: The lichen dragon katydid from the modern Ecuadorian Andes provides an excellent disguise of lichens.
source: An extraordinary orthopteran, the lichen dragon katydid from the modern Ecuadorian Andes, provides an excellent disguise of lichens (Braun, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Braun, 2011.

claim: Extant chrysopid larvae have a body mask adorned with affixed lichen fragments.
source: Other predatory and extant chrysopid larvae have a body mask adorned with affixed lichen fragments, an example of aggressive mimicry or the 'wolf in sheep's clothing' syndrome (Skorepa and Sharp, 1971; Slocum and Lawrey, 1976; Wilson and Methven, 1997; Tauber et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to published studies on chrysopid larvae behavior.

claim: Lichen-mimetic or -camouflaged insects have established a specialized lichen-association for feeding or sheltering to obtain survival advantage.
source: Importantly, lichen-mimetic or -camouflaged insects have established a specialized lichen-association for feeding or sheltering to obtain survival advantage (Gerson, 1973).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Gerson, 1973.

claim: This finding documents the earliest lichen-mimicking insect.
source: Our finding documents the earliest lichen-mimicking insect and reveals that this strategy of mimicry among insects has been in existence for minimally 165 Mya.
evidence: This is based on the age of the fossil specimens and comparison with other known examples of lichen mimicry.

claim: The strategy of lichen mimicry among insects has been in existence for minimally 165 Mya.
source: Our finding documents the earliest lichen-mimicking insect and reveals that this strategy of mimicry among insects has been in existence for minimally 165 Mya.
evidence: This is based on the age of the fossil deposit (168-152 Ma).

claim: Five fossil lichen specimens were studied: PB23120, B0474, B0476P/C, CNU-LICHEN-NN2019001 and CNU-LICHEN-NN2019002P/C.
source: We have studied five fossil lichen specimens, PB23120, B0474, B0476P/C, CNU-LICHEN-NN2019001 and CNU-LICHEN-NN2019002P/C, all of which were collected from the Daohugou 1 locality of Inner Mongolia.
evidence: This is based on the specimens examined in the study.

claim: All studied lichen specimens were collected from the Daohugou 1 locality of Inner Mongolia.
source: We have studied five fossil lichen specimens, PB23120, B0474, B0476P/C, CNU-LICHEN-NN2019001 and CNU-LICHEN-NN2019002P/C, all of which were collected from the Daohugou 1 locality of Inner Mongolia.
evidence: This is based on the collection data for the specimens.

claim: The newly collected specimens were identified as Daohugouthallus ciliiferus based on careful observations of its distinctive morphology.
source: The newly collected specimens were identified to be Daohugouthallus ciliiferus based on careful observations of its distinctive morphology.
evidence: This is based on morphological examination of the specimens.

claim: D. ciliiferus has a thallus that is foliose to subfruticose.
source: Thallus foliose to subfruticose; lobes ca. 20–30 mm long, irregularly branched, margin sometimes revolute; lateral and terminal branches ca. 0.5–5.0 mm long, tips tapered; upper surface smooth, partly broken; aggregated black spots often present, punctiform; cilia sometimes present near the branch tips, forming filiform appendages; lobules occasionally present (Figure 1).
evidence: This is based on morphological observations of the fossil specimens shown in Figure 1.

claim: D. ciliiferus lobes are ca. 20–30 mm long and irregularly branched.
source: Thallus foliose to subfruticose; lobes ca. 20–30 mm long, irregularly branched, margin sometimes revolute; lateral and terminal branches ca. 0.5–5.0 mm long, tips tapered; upper surface smooth, partly broken; aggregated black spots often present, punctiform; cilia sometimes present near the branch tips, forming filiform appendages; lobules occasionally present (Figure 1).
evidence: This is based on measurements of the fossil specimens.

claim: D. ciliiferus has lateral and terminal branches ca. 0.5–5.0 mm long with tapered tips.
source: Thallus foliose to subfruticose; lobes ca. 20–30 mm long, irregularly branched, margin sometimes revolute; lateral and terminal branches ca. 0.5–5.0 mm long, tips tapered; upper surface smooth, partly broken; aggregated black spots often present, punctiform; cilia sometimes present near the branch tips, forming filiform appendages; lobules occasionally present (Figure 1).
evidence: This is based on measurements and observations of the fossil specimens.

claim: D. ciliiferus has aggregated black spots that are often present and punctiform.
source: Thallus foliose to subfruticose; lobes ca. 20–30 mm long, irregularly branched, margin sometimes revolute; lateral and terminal branches ca. 0.5–5.0 mm long, tips tapered; upper surface smooth, partly broken; aggregated black spots often present, punctiform; cilia sometimes present near the branch tips, forming filiform appendages; lobules occasionally present (Figure 1).
evidence: This is based on observations of the fossil specimens shown in Figure 1.

claim: D. ciliiferus has an upper cortex that is conglutinate, comprising one cell layer, very thin, ca. 1 μm thick.
source: Upper cortex conglutinate, comprising one cell layer, very thin, ca. 1 μm thick (Figure 2A); algal cells globose to near globose, one-celled, mostly 1.5–2.1 μm in diameter, some in framboidal form, interconnected (Figure 2A,B,F) by or adhered (Figure 2C–H) to the fungal hyphae with simple wall-to-wall mycobiont-photobiont interface; fungal hyphae filamentous, some shriveled, septate (Figure 2B,C,G,H), 1.2–1.5 μm wide.
evidence: This is based on SEM observations shown in Figure 2A.

claim: D. ciliiferus has algal cells that are globose to near globose, one-celled, mostly 1.5–2.1 μm in diameter.
source: Upper cortex conglutinate, comprising one cell layer, very thin, ca. 1 μm thick (Figure 2A); algal cells globose to near globose, one-celled, mostly 1.5–2.1 μm in diameter, some in framboidal form, interconnected (Figure 2A,B,F) by or adhered (Figure 2C–H) to the fungal hyphae with simple wall-to-wall mycobiont-photobiont interface; fungal hyphae filamentous, some shriveled, septate (Figure 2B,C,G,H), 1.2–1.5 μm wide.
evidence: This is based on SEM observations and measurements shown in Figure 2.

claim: Some algal cells of D. ciliiferus are in framboidal form and interconnected by or adhered to fungal hyphae.
source: Upper cortex conglutinate, comprising one cell layer, very thin, ca. 1 μm thick (Figure 2A); algal cells globose to near globose, one-celled, mostly 1.5–2.1 μm in diameter, some in framboidal form, interconnected (Figure 2A,B,F) by or adhered (Figure 2C–H) to the fungal hyphae with simple wall-to-wall mycobiont-photobiont interface; fungal hyphae filamentous, some shriveled, septate (Figure 2B,C,G,H), 1.2–1.5 μm wide.
evidence: This is based on SEM observations shown in Figure 2.

claim: D. ciliiferus has fungal hyphae that are filamentous, some shriveled, septate, and 1.2–1.5 μm wide.
source: Upper cortex conglutinate, comprising one cell layer, very thin, ca. 1 μm thick (Figure 2A); algal cells globose to near globose, one-celled, mostly 1.5–2.1 μm in diameter, some in framboidal form, interconnected (Figure 2A,B,F) by or adhered (Figure 2C–H) to the fungal hyphae with simple wall-to-wall mycobiont-photobiont interface; fungal hyphae filamentous, some shriveled, septate (Figure 2B,C,G,H), 1.2–1.5 μm wide.
evidence: This is based on SEM observations and measurements shown in Figure 2.

claim: Daohugouthallus ciliiferus was reported by Wang et al., 2010a as a new genus and new species of lichen.
source: This adpression lichen fossil was reported by Wang et al., 2010a as a new genus and new species of lichen, that is Daohugouthallus ciliiferus.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Wang et al., 2010a.

claim: The lichen affinity of D. ciliiferus was doubted and thought as ambiguous because no anatomic characters including both fungal and algal components were provided.
source: However, there were no anatomic characters including both fungal and algal components that was provided and consequently its lichen affinity was doubted and thought as ambiguous (Honegger et al., 2013; Lücking and Nelsen, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Honegger et al., 2013 and Lücking and Nelsen, 2018.

claim: A lichen fossil should accord with three important criteria: presence of a mycobiont component, presence of a photobiont component, and presence of spatial connections between both components.
source: Actually, the lichen fossil now has been well defined and should accord with three important criteria: presence of a mycobiont component, presence of a photobiont component, and presence of spatial connections between both components (Lücking and Nelsen, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Lücking and Nelsen, 2018.

claim: The algal cells of D. ciliiferus are similar to Trebouxia of Chlorolichenomycites salopensis in morphology but much smaller.
source: Second, the algal cells are globose and occasionally have a spherical assembly of microcrystals in framboidal form similar to Trebouxia of Chlorolichenomycites salopensis in morphology but much smaller (Honegger et al., 2013).
evidence: This is based on comparison with published descriptions and is supported by a citation to Honegger et al., 2013.

claim: The spatial connections between fungal hyphae and algal cells of D. ciliiferus have been observed, mostly consisting of fungal hyphae interweaved with algal cells.
source: Third, the spatial connections between fungal hyphae and algal cells have been observed, mostly consisting of fungal hyphae interweaved with algal cells (Figure 2A,C,D,F).
evidence: This is based on SEM observations shown in Figure 2.

claim: The characters of Daohugouthallus ciliiferus accord well with the definition of lichen fossil and indicate a strong affinity to a lichen.
source: The above-mentioned characters of Daohugouthallus ciliiferus accords well with the definition of lichen fossil and indicate a strong affinity to a lichen.
evidence: This is inferred from the anatomical observations presented in the manuscript.

claim: Daohugouthallus ciliiferus would be easily associated with extant Everniastrum cirrhatum from external morphology.
source: From the external morphology, Daohugouthallus ciliiferus would be easily associated with extant Everniastrum cirrhatum, a conclusion that requires further study in the near future.
evidence: This is based on morphological comparison and is presented as speculation requiring further study.

claim: The lichen-mimicking insects represent a new genus and two new species affiliated to Ithonidae of the order Neuroptera.
source: The lichen-mimicking insects represent a new genus and two new species affiliated to Ithonidae of the order Neuroptera.
evidence: This is based on the taxonomic analysis and description presented in the manuscript.

claim: Lichenipolystoechotes angustimaculatus is the type species of the new genus.
source: Lichenipolystoechotes angustimaculatus Fang, Zheng et Wang, sp. nov. (type species), Lichenipolystoechotes ramimaculatus Fang, Ma et Wang, sp. nov.
evidence: This is stated in the taxonomic description.

claim: The new genus Lichenipolystoechotes has a forewing that is ellipsoidal shaped, medium length, slightly narrow with length-width ratio 3.25–3.5.
source: Forewing ellipsoidal shaped, medium length, slightly narrow with length-width ratio 3.25–3.5; membrane bearing coralliform pattern with unclosed diaphanous U-shaped fenestrae along the margin in forewing; costal space slightly broad basally, then narrowed towards wing apex; ScA and recurved humeral veinlet present; costal cross-veins simple in proximal half, and then distally forked; ScP and RA fused distally, ending close to the wing apex, no cross-veins present in this area; cross-veins in area between RA and RP scattered; RP with about 18 branches, RP1 a single branch, few cross-veins scattered at the radial sector; M forked beyond the separation point of RP1, MA and MP with the similar branched pattern, the number of MP branches slightly more than MA; CuA distinctly multi-forked, with 7–10 pectinate branches; CuP bifurcated.
evidence: This is based on morphological measurements and observations of the fossil specimens.

claim: The new genus can easily be assigned to Ithonidae by the following characters: medium body size, prolonged forewing, relatively narrow costal space, and presence of ScA and recurrent humeral veinlet.
source: The new genus can easily be assigned to Ithonidae by the following characters: medium body size, prolonged forewing, relatively narrow costal space, and presence of ScA and recurrent humeral veinlet.
evidence: This is based on comparison with known characters of Ithonidae.

claim: The forewing characters of the new genus conform to a polystoechotid affiliation.
source: In addition, its forewing characters, including Sc and R1 fused distally, few cross-veins except for a row of well-defined outer gradate series in radial sector, MP forked beyond MA divergence, conforming to a polystoechotid affiliation (Zheng et al., 2016).
evidence: This is based on comparison with polystoechotid characters and is supported by a citation to Zheng et al., 2016.

claim: The new genus is distinguished from other polystoechotid genera by the distinctive coralliform markings of the forewings.
source: It also is distinguished from other polystoechotid genera by the distinctive coralliform markings of the forewings.
evidence: This is based on morphological comparison with other polystoechotid genera.

claim: L. angustimaculatus has a forewing that is elongate, oval shaped, about 21.3 mm long, 6.5 mm wide.
source: Forewing elongate, oval shaped, about 21.3 mm long, 6.5 mm wide; membrane bearing irregular coralloid markings of pigmentation, forming many diaphanous marginal fenestrae; costal space slightly broad basally, then narrowed towards the wing apex; costal cross-veins scarcely branched in proximal half of wing, and then forming bifurcated branches in distal half; sc-ra cross-vein absent; space between RA and RP relatively narrow with seven cross-veins; RP with 18 pectinate branches, and each branch bifurcated near wing margin; cross-veins in radial sector relatively scarce except for the middle gradate series; M forked slightly beyond the separation of RP1; MA and MP forming seven pectinate branches each; CuA pectinate branched in distal half part, forming seven pectinate branches; CuP first bifurcated at the proximal half, then forming the distal simple forks; A1–A3 forming several pectinate branches; a few cross-veins present among MA and A3.
evidence: This is based on measurements of the holotype specimen.

claim: L. ramimaculatus has a forewing that is elongate, oval shaped, about 22.8 mm long, 6.5 mm wide.
source: Forewing elongate, oval shaped, about 22.8 mm long, 6.5 mm wide; costal space slightly broadened, then narrowed towards wing apex; subcostal veinlets relatively widely spaced, scarcely branched medially, forming multiple bifurcated branches distally; areas between Sc and RA narrow, without crossveins; space between RA and RP relatively narrow with sparse crossveins; RP with about 22 pectinate branches; RP1 branched from RP near wing base, single until wing margin; M forked basally, MA forming two distal dichotomous branches, and MP forming six distal pectinate branches; CuA pectinate medially to distally, forming 11 pectinate branches; CuP bifurcated at middle; A1–A3 partly preserved.
evidence: This is based on measurements of the holotype specimen.

claim: The two new species of Lichenipolystoechotes can be separated by the distinct differences of branches of the MA and CuA veins.
source: The two new species of Lichenipolystoechotes exhibit a very similar appearance, but they easily can be separated by the distinct differences of branches of the MA and CuA veins.
evidence: This is based on morphological comparison of the two species.

claim: Lichenipolystoechotes species are conspicuous based on their highly prominent, homologous, pigmentation pattern of their forewings.
source: Lichenipolystoechotes species are conspicuous based on their highly prominent, homologous, pigmentation pattern of their forewings, which implies that these insects evolved a similar defensive strategy.
evidence: This is based on morphological observations and is inferred to relate to defensive strategy.

claim: The closest extant relatives of Lichenipolystoechotes are Ithonidae (moth lacewings).
source: The closest extant relatives of Lichenipolystoechotes are Ithonidae (moth lacewings), of which their ecological and biological features are poorly documented (New, 1989).
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic affinity and is supported by a citation to New, 1989.

claim: The forewings of the two new species demonstrate a high similarity in their overall appearance to the thallus branches of the co-occurring foliose to subfruticose lichen Daohugouthallus ciliiferus.
source: The forewings of the two new species demonstrate a high similarity in their overall appearance, such as the forewing branching pattern (Figures 3A,E and 4A) that matches the thallus branches of the co-occurring foliose to subfruticose lichen Daohugouthallus ciliiferus (Figure 4B–D; Wang et al., 2010a).
evidence: This is based on morphological comparison shown in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: The entire forewing forms an irregular branching pattern amid rounded, diaphanous fenestrae that are distributed along the wing center and as U-shaped extensions occurring around the wing border.
source: The entire forewing forms an irregular branching pattern amid rounded, diaphanous fenestrae (windows) that are distributed along the wing center and as U-shaped extensions occurring around the wing border.
evidence: This is based on morphological observations of the fossil specimens.

claim: The variation in width of each forewing vein branch conforms well to the variation in width of the lichen's branches.
source: The variation in width of each forewing vein branch conforms well to the variation in width of the lichen's branches, indicating a morphological similarity between the wing markings and lichen thallus (Figure 4F; Figure 4—figure supplement 1; Supplementary file 1: Table S1).
evidence: This is based on quantitative measurements shown in Figure 4F and Supplementary file 1.

claim: Lichens often have punctiform pycnidia with black spots appearing on their thallus, especially in extant foliose lichen families such as Parmeliaceae.
source: Lichens often have punctiform pycnidia (asexual reproductive structures) with black spots appearing on their thallus, especially in extant foliose lichen families such as Parmeliaceae (Thell et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Thell et al., 2012.

claim: A specimen of L. ramimaculatus displays similar, scattered spots on its wings that resemble the dark spots on the lichen thallus of D. ciliiferus.
source: It is noteworthy that a specimen of L. ramimaculatus displays similar, scattered spots on its wings that resemble the dark spots on the lichen thallus of D. ciliiferus (Figure 4G–I), potentially strengthening the similarity between L. ramimaculatus and D. ciliiferus.
evidence: This is based on morphological observations shown in Figure 4G-I.

claim: The details of insect morphology likely enhanced the similarity of the insect with a co-occurring lichen, providing a reasonable inference that the forewing is mimetic with the lichen thallus.
source: Collectively, these details of insect morphology likely enhanced the similarity of the insect with a co-occurring lichen, providing a reasonable inference that the forewing is mimetic with the lichen thallus.
evidence: This is inferred from the morphological similarities documented in the manuscript.

claim: Lichens are stable, symbiotic associations of fungi and algae.
source: It is generally known that lichens are stable, symbiotic associations of fungi and algae (Lücking and Nelsen, 2018).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation to Lücking and Nelsen, 2018.

claim: Lichens are regarded as pioneers in the colonization of novel surfaces such as bark, rock and soil.
source: At the same time, lichens are regarded as pioneers in the colonization of novel surfaces such as bark, rock and soil, which dominate about 7% of the earth's terrestrial surface (Larson, 1987), and have a distribution from the polar regions to the tropics (Lumbsch and Rikkinen, 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to Larson, 1987 and Lumbsch and Rikkinen, 2017.

claim: Lichens dominate about 7% of the earth's terrestrial surface.
source: At the same time, lichens are regarded as pioneers in the colonization of novel surfaces such as bark, rock and soil, which dominate about 7% of the earth's terrestrial surface (Larson, 1987), and have a distribution from the polar regions to the tropics (Lumbsch and Rikkinen, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Larson, 1987.

claim: Lichens have a distribution from the polar regions to the tropics.
source: At the same time, lichens are regarded as pioneers in the colonization of novel surfaces such as bark, rock and soil, which dominate about 7% of the earth's terrestrial surface (Larson, 1987), and have a distribution from the polar regions to the tropics (Lumbsch and Rikkinen, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Lumbsch and Rikkinen, 2017.

claim: Lichens are prominent in arctic-alpine vegetation types in wet and higher montane forests.
source: They are prominent in arctic-alpine vegetation types in wet and higher montane forests (Lumbsch and Rikkinen, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Lumbsch and Rikkinen, 2017.

claim: Many extant foliose or fruticose lichens such as taxa of Parmeliaceae are known to be epiphytic or corticolous.
source: Many extant foliose or fruticose lichens such as taxa of Parmeliaceae are known to be epiphytic or corticolous, and bark surfaces are one of the most common substrates (Lumbsch and Rikkinen, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Lumbsch and Rikkinen, 2017.

claim: Daohugouthallus ciliiferus is considered an epiphytic foliose to subfruticose lichen.
source: Daohugouthallus ciliiferus is considered an epiphytic foliose to subfruticose lichen, and often is found entangled with gymnosperm seed cones (Figures 1C and 4D; Wang et al., 2010a).
evidence: This is based on observations of the fossil specimens and is supported by a citation to Wang et al., 2010a.

claim: D. ciliiferus is often found entangled with gymnosperm seed cones.
source: Daohugouthallus ciliiferus is considered an epiphytic foliose to subfruticose lichen, and often is found entangled with gymnosperm seed cones (Figures 1C and 4D; Wang et al., 2010a).
evidence: This is based on observations of the fossil specimens shown in Figures 1C and 4D and is supported by a citation to Wang et al., 2010a.

claim: When Lichenipolystoechotes moth lacewings reposed in a habitat rich in D. ciliiferus, a near perfect match of their appearances would assist their concealment.
source: When Lichenipolystoechotes moth lacewings reposed in a habitat rich in D. ciliiferus, a near perfect match of their appearances would assist their concealment.
evidence: This is inferred from the morphological similarities between the insect and lichen.

claim: Some larvae of green lacewings carry packets of lichen material on their backs to hide themselves.
source: Among extant Neuroptera, similar appearances of lichen-camouflage or related cases have been recorded in some larvae of green lacewings that carry packets of lichen material on their backs to hide themselves (Slocum and Lawrey, 1976; Wilson and Methven, 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Slocum and Lawrey, 1976 and Wilson and Methven, 1997.

claim: Lichenipolystoechotes likely acquired a similar survival advantage when they occupied a lichen-rich habitat.
source: Although Lichenipolystoechotes probably lacked the same life-habit as modern lichen-carrying chrysopoid larvae, the Jurassic taxa likely acquired a similar survival advantage when they occupied a lichen-rich habitat.
evidence: This is inferred from comparison with modern lichen-carrying larvae.

claim: Some extant Thyridosmylus species of Osmylidae possess similar complex wing markings and often occur on moss-laden surfaces of rocks, tree bark and indurated soil surfaces.
source: Some extant Thyridosmylus species of Osmylidae, another archaic lineage of Neuroptera, possess similar complex wing markings and often occur on moss-laden surfaces of rocks, tree bark and indurated soil surfaces (Winterton et al., 2017; Figure 2B), which exhibit an impressive consistency with their surroundings (pers. observ. by Yongjie Wang).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Winterton et al., 2017 and personal observation.

claim: Modern lichens can produce a variety of lichenic acids that are unpalatable to many insects.
source: Modern lichens can produce a variety of lichenic acids (Gerson, 1973) that are unpalatable to many insects and enhance the protective sheltering for animals.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Gerson, 1973.

claim: A micro-ecosystem of lichens and lichen-tolerant animals existed 165 million-years-ago in Northeastern China.
source: We hypothesize that such a micro-ecosystem existed 165 million-years-ago in Northeastern China that accommodated these trophic, sheltering, defensive and mimetic interactions.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the fossil evidence presented in the study.

claim: The industrial melanism of the peppered moth Biston betularia in nineteenth century Britain is an iconic case of lichen and insect resemblance.
source: Although lichen mimesis is not well documented among extant insects, the most iconic such case of lichen and insect resemblance is the industrial melanism of the peppered moth Biston betularia in nineteenth century Britain (Gerson, 1973; Stevens, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Gerson, 1973 and Stevens, 2011.

claim: The Industrial Revolution caused elevated levels of soot laden air pollution that resulted in disappearance of lichen shelters for the light-colored morph of B. betularia.
source: The Industrial Revolution caused elevated levels of soot laden air pollution that resulted in disappearance of lichen shelters for the light-colored morph of B. betularia, as their corresponding habitation sites were changed from lightly tinged to dark-hued lichen surfaces that led to their greater vulnerability to predation.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the industrial melanism case study.

claim: Selection pressures such as predation by birds genuinely affected the differential survival of the pale and dark colored morphs of B. betularia under differently hued backgrounds.
source: Nevertheless, other studies demonstrated that selection pressures such as predation by birds genuinely affected the differential survival of the pale and dark colored morphs of B. betularia under differently hued backgrounds (Howlett and Majerus, 1987; Liebert and Brakefield, 1987; Majerus, 2009; Walton and Stevens, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to published studies on B. betularia.

claim: The Jurassic Lichenipolystoechotes could have gained survival advantage from mimesis of a lichen similar to that of modern B. betularia–lichen mimesis.
source: It is possible that the Jurassic Lichenipolystoechotes could have gained survival advantage from mimesis of a lichen similar to that of modern B. betularia–lichen mimesis.
evidence: This is speculation based on comparison with the B. betularia case.

claim: High-contrast lichen-like markings could contribute to concealment of the insects.
source: If so, high-contrast lichen-like markings could contribute to concealment of the insects.
evidence: This is speculation about the function of the wing markings.

claim: High-contrast markings of Lichenipolystoechotes species can be interpreted as disruptive coloration.
source: Alternatively, such high-contrast markings of Lichenipolystoechotes species also can be interpreted as disruptive coloration, which would confuse the boundaries of moth lacewing and lichen to prevent the detection of a body part essential for survival (Stevens, 2011).
evidence: This is speculation about an alternative function of the markings, supported by a citation to Stevens, 2011.

claim: The lichen-like markings of Lichenipolystoechotes could likely bring double protections to the insects: background mimicry and disruptive coloration.
source: Consequently, the lichen-like markings of Lichenipolystoechotes could likely bring the double protections to the insects-background mimicry and disruptive coloration.
evidence: This is speculation about the dual function of the wing markings.

claim: Some modern insects such as ants, dipterans and larva of green lacewings are considered to potentially contribute to dispersal of lichens by transporting lichen propagules to new sites of colonization.
source: Some modern insects such as ants, dipterans and larva of green lacewings are considered to potentially contribute to dispersal of lichens by transporting lichen propagules to new sites of colonization (Gerson, 1973; Keller and Scheidegger, 2016; Ronnås et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Gerson, 1973; Keller and Scheidegger, 2016; and Ronnås et al., 2017.

claim: Lichenipolystoechotes possessed a considerably larger body size that likely was convenient for dispersal of lichen propagules.
source: In a comparison with such relatively small, lichen-carrying insects, Lichenipolystoechotes possessed a considerably larger body size that likely was convenient for dispersal of lichen propagules.
evidence: This is speculation based on the body size of the fossil insects.

claim: Sexual reproductive organs such as apothecia have not been found on the D. ciliiferus thallus.
source: Notably, sexual reproductive organs such as apothecia have not been found on the D. ciliiferus thallus based on light-microscopic morphological and SEM anatomical observations; neither were vegetative propagules such as soredia or isidia seen except along marginal lobules that occasionally were present.
evidence: This is based on observations of the fossil specimens.

claim: Vegetative propagules such as soredia or isidia were not seen on D. ciliiferus except along marginal lobules that occasionally were present.
source: Notably, sexual reproductive organs such as apothecia have not been found on the D. ciliiferus thallus based on light-microscopic morphological and SEM anatomical observations; neither were vegetative propagules such as soredia or isidia seen except along marginal lobules that occasionally were present.
evidence: This is based on observations of the fossil specimens.

claim: As predaceous insects, Lichenipolystoechotes inhabited a lichen-rich environment to evade their predators, but they also could have predated and consumed smaller lichen-feeding animals while simultaneously decreasing herbivore damage to the D. ciliiferus thallus.
source: As predaceous insects, Lichenipolystoechotes inhabited a lichen-rich environment to evade their predators, but they also could have predated and consumed smaller lichen-feeding animals while simultaneously decreasing herbivore damage to the D. ciliiferus thallus.
evidence: This is speculation about the ecological role of Lichenipolystoechotes.

claim: The accepted oldest lichen fossil was reported from the Early Devonian.
source: The accepted oldest lichen fossil was reported from the Early Devonian and lichens have existed minimally for 410 million years (Taylor et al., 1995; Honegger et al., 2013; Lücking and Nelsen, 2018), as have the apterygote insects (Misof et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Taylor et al., 1995; Honegger et al., 2013; and Lücking and Nelsen, 2018.

claim: Lichens have existed minimally for 410 million years.
source: The accepted oldest lichen fossil was reported from the Early Devonian and lichens have existed minimally for 410 million years (Taylor et al., 1995; Honegger et al., 2013; Lücking and Nelsen, 2018), as have the apterygote insects (Misof et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Taylor et al., 1995; Honegger et al., 2013; and Lücking and Nelsen, 2018.

claim: Apterygote insects have existed for at least 410 million years.
source: The accepted oldest lichen fossil was reported from the Early Devonian and lichens have existed minimally for 410 million years (Taylor et al., 1995; Honegger et al., 2013; Lücking and Nelsen, 2018), as have the apterygote insects (Misof et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Misof et al., 2014.

claim: This report describes the oldest examples of lichen mimesis that involved two lacewing species resembling a contemporaneous lichen from the same, latest Middle Jurassic deposit.
source: Although there is virtually no evidence to suggest when and how such association began; in this report, we describe the oldest examples of lichen mimesis that involved two lacewing species resembling a contemporaneous lichen from the same, latest Middle Jurassic deposit.
evidence: This is based on the fossil evidence presented in the manuscript.

claim: These insect lineages have acquired mimicry association with lichens in less than half of the time (40%) of the duration of both major lineages since the early Devonian.
source: These insect lineages have acquired mimicry association with lichens in less than half of the time (40%) of the duration of both major lineages since the early Devonian (Figure 6).
evidence: This is calculated based on the age of the fossil (165 Ma) relative to the origin of lichens and insects (410 Ma).

claim: Specimens were collected from the Daohugou 1 locality of the Jiulongshan Formation, near Daohugou Village, Ningcheng County, Inner Mongolia, China.
source: Specimens were collected from the Daohugou 1 locality of the Jiulongshan Formation, near Daohugou Village, Ningcheng County, approximately 80 km south of Chifeng City, in the Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region, China (119°14.318′E, 41°18.979′N).
evidence: This is based on the collection data for the specimens.

claim: The age of the Jiulongshan Formation is 168–152 Ma based on 40Ar/39Ar and 206Pb/238U isotopic analyses.
source: The age of this formation is 168–152 Ma based on 40Ar/39Ar and 206Pb/238U isotopic analyses (Hy et al., 2004; Liu, 2006; Ren, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Hy et al., 2004; Liu, 2006; and Ren, 2019.
